title: The Deer Hunter just might be the best film about Vietnam, even better than Apocalypse Now

commenti.body: [removed]

I think Deer Hunter is a much more personable film, as we go full in-depth with Mike, Nick and Steve before they are taken off to Vietnam, so what happens to them as much more of impact. 

Whereas in Apocalypse Now, we are introduced to an already hardened Willard, and the the men on the boat we only have some time to learn about, as most of the film is focused on Willard investigating Kurtz’ character and what lead to him going insane. 

The films are really about two different things: Deer Hunter is more about the psychological effects war has on a person and how it changes them after a conflict, whereas Apocalypse Now was really about the all round madness of the Vietnam War  and the darkness lurking in a person’s soul (echoing its source material, The Heart of Darkness).

Apocalypse now is a reimagining of heart of darkness. Deer Hunter was released 3 years after the end of the  war & is about the impact of the war on the people involved in it. They're not really the same thing imo, although I do understand the comparison. To be honest I cannot think of any other Vietnam film has dealt with this topic as well as deer hunter. Platoon was comic book good vs evil. Full metal jacket was about training. Most others are just out & out action movies...and so it goes on, the only film I think attempts to deal with the same topic is born on the fourth of july. But the impact of the deer hunter, so painfully close to the war itself, is unique.

I wouldn’t call Apocalypse Now a film about Vietnam in the same way Deer Hunter is about Vietnam. With AN it’s more of just a setting for exploring themes of insanity, chaos, war, etc. The novel has nothing to do with Vietnam. But yes, as far as which one tells a story more specific to how the Vietnam War affected American lives, Deer Hunter is going to be the one.

Follow the conversation:

Speaker A suggests that Apocalypse Now and The Deer Hunter are "the two definitive and best films on the [Vietnam] war."

Speaker B (me) suggests, albeit bluntly, that those two films are only interested in offering the US perspective on the war.


Sounds more reductive than definitive to me, but perhaps it's a matter of being pedantic about language. If Speaker A had said that the films were the definitive and best regarding _the US perspective_ that would've been more agreeable.

Really my train of thought would be, it does everyone some good to watch more non-American cinema in general and offers perspective outside of what might be considered by any one country to be "definitive" (or worst of all, "correct.")

The reasons for, horrors of, and eventual outcomes from any such conflict would be myriad and rippling, affecting generations in unfathomable ways. So, no, neither film is likely to be definitive of the entire history in and of itself, certainly less so when it is seen solely from one perspective.

It's a huge comment to make that actually might undermine the real traumas and realities of those involved and those affected.

And to equate that due to the source material Apocalypse Now is still about the Belgian Congo is dumb as rocks and you know it. Ain't nobody watching that and going "yeah, but it's _actually about Belgium_, you know."

The Deer Hunter is a little more conventional and a little more palatable because of its simplistic story. There’s good guys, there’s bad guys, one gets addicted to drugs to cope with his trauma and his friend goes back to rescue him. It’s a great story, it’s entertaining, well done and superbly acted by some of the greatest actors of a generation. But it’s straightforward and not thought provoking. War is bad, it hurts people and there’s sometimes heroes, fade to black. 

Apocalypse Now is morally complex. We see it in the helicopter attack on a seemingly peaceful North Vietnamese. We see it with Kilgore who cares about his men and then even go as far to let a dying enemy combatant drink from his canteen before abandoning him to surf. Willard debates this internally, what purpose does killing Kurtz actually serve? Who is Kurtz really? Kurtz is a madman but also correct in that the was is madness, all sides are morally corrupt. He’s gone insane trying to create his own authoritarian utopia. The duality of who he is is visible; there’s bodies hanging from trees yet children adore playing with Kurtz and other adults worship him as a God. 

There’s no heroes and no villains in Apocalypse Now. Willard debates his own morality in a drug and alcohol induced hazed. The North Vietnamese are shown as primitive, they fight with arrows and crude bombs. 

Cinematically Apocalypse Now is far better. It’s truly an epic. The Deer Hunter has that 70s technicolor look, there’s no stedicam shots, the soundtrack is a little sappy.

I think the Deer Hunter has its place in the cinematic landscape and is worthy of praise. It was the first view into what Vietnam veterans experienced. But Apocalypse Now is far better. It’s a true work of art and there’s a strong case for it being the best American War movie of all time.

I disagree that FMJ was solely about training. It's more of a general exploration of the process of how young men are turned into hardened killers ("thousand yard stare", "duality of man" etc). However, most audiences, including contemporary critics, were so invested in the first half and Vincent D'Onofrios stellar performance, that they didn't really get the subtler symbolism of the second half.

I think Kubrick fans and scholars have started to appreciate it more fully again. Like any Kubrick movie it teems with more symbolism in every frame and line than you'd notice upon first watch. I'm not gonna mention all of them but for example Kubrick comments on the vital role of wartime sexual assault in breaking an ordinary young man into a hardened killer. The soldiers use the phrase "boom boom" to refer both to sex, as in the scene with the prostitute, and to killing, when Joker mercykills the sniper girl. Joker also expresses disgust at the death of women and children throughout the story, especially in the chopper scene, but the movie culminates in him killing a female child soldier.

A lot of people seem to miss that Kubrick seemingly wanted to make a more general exploration of how war changes young men, and assume this is another film criticizing the Vietnam War or the US specifically. Sure there's bits of that but it's far from the core message. Also it's a really fun movie. Hot take but it's better than A Clockwork Orange and Eyes Wide Shut. Also the Mickey Mouse Clubhouse ending is one of the best and most chilling Kubrick ever made

O brother used the Great Depression to retell Homers odyssey. In Apoclypse, they use Nam as a way to retell Heart of Darkness.

I have the same reaction to this film, haha!  My grandmother was from Western Pennsylvania and a large family of Russian immigrants.  (I looked up her birth place and it's not even technically a settlement.)  All Russian Orthodox.  Both my grandmother and my mother said the wedding scene in *The Deer Hunter* was exactly like the weddings they attended in Pennsylvania growing up.  *The Deer Hunter* apparently nailed Russian Orthodox Pennsyltucky.
